problem.paragraph: A genetic trait is often governed by a pair of genes, one inherited from each parent. The genes may be of two types, often labeled A and a. An individual then may have three different pairs: AA, Aa (which is the same as aA), or aa. In many cases the AA and Aa individuals cannot be otherwise distinguished; in these cases gene A is dominant and gene a is recessive. Likewise, an AA individual is called dominant and an aa individual is called recessive. An Aa individual is called a hybrid.

list.item: Show that if a dominant individual is mated with a hybrid, the probability of an offspring being dominant is $$1/2$$ and the probability of an offspring being a hybrid is $$1/2$$ .
Show that if a recessive individual is mated with a hybrid, the probability of an offspring being recessive is $$1/2$$ and the probability of an offspring being a hybrid is $$1/2$$ .

Show that if a hybrid individual is mated with another hybrid, the probability of an offspring being dominant is $$1/4$$ , the probability of an offspring being recessive is $$1/4$$ , and the probability of an offspring being a hybrid is $$1/2$$ .

problem.paragraph: By Theorem 1(e), all eigenvalues $$\text{λ}$$ of a regular matrix other than $$1$$ have the property that $$| \text{λ} | < 1$$ ; that is, the eigenvalue $$1$$ is a strictly dominant eigenvalue. Suppose that $$\textbf{x}_{0} = c_{1}\textbf{q} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + \cdots + c_{n}\textbf{v}_{n}$$ is a linear combination of eigenvectors of $$P$$ .

list.item: Use Equation (2) in Section 5.8 to derive an expression for $$\textbf{x}_{k} = P^{k}\textbf{x}_{0}$$ .

list.item: Since $$P^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 4 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 2 \\ 1 / 2 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 4 \\ 1 / 4 & 1 / 2 & 1 / 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ $$P$$ is regular by the definition with $$k = 2$$ .

Solve the equation $$P\textbf{q} = \textbf{q}$$ , which may be rewritten as $$(P - I)\textbf{q} = \textbf{0}$$ . Since $$P - I = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 / 2 & 0 & 1 / 2 \\ 1 / 2 & - 1 / 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 / 2 & - 1 / 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ and row reducing the augmented matrix gives $$\begin{bmatrix} - 1 / 2 & 0 & 1 / 2 & 0 \\ 1 / 2 & - 1 / 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 / 2 & - 1 / 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & - 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ the general solution is $$q_{3}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Since $$\textbf{q}$$ must be a probability vector, set $$q_{3} = 1/(1 + 1 + 1) = 1/3$$ and compute that $$\text{q} = \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \text{1} / \text{3} \\ \text{1} / \text{3} \\ 1 / 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
The chain will spend $$1/3$$ of its time in state $$2$$ since the entry in $$\textbf{q}$$ corresponding to state $$2$$ is $$1/3$$ , and we can interpret the entries as occupation times.
